Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 103, verses 1–3:

It is Meccan according to the majority.

Qatadah said: it is Medinan.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Asr was revealed in Makkah."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Abu Muzaynah al-Darimi, who had companionship with the Prophet, that he said: "When two men from among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) met, they would not part until one of them recited Surat al-Asr to the other, and then one of them would greet the other with salam."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Allah swears by al-Asr, and it is al-dahr (time), because of the lessons in it from the passing of night and day according to the measured stages and the succession of darkness and light. Indeed, in that there is a clear proof of the Creator, mighty and majestic, and of His oneness. It is said that al-layl (night) is called 'asr and al-nahar (day) is called 'asr, and from this is the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"The two 'asrs did not cease, a day and a night, when they sought to overtake what they wished."

It is also said that al-ghadah (morning) and al-'ashi (evening) are called two 'asrs, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"I keep delaying him with the two 'asrs until he tires of me, and he accepts half the debt while his nose is still rubbed in the dust."

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: what is meant in the verse is al-'ashi, which is the period between the decline of the sun and its setting, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Amr goes forth with us, and he has shortened the 'asr; in the first going forth is the spoil and the reward."

It is also narrated from Qatadah that it is the last hour of the hours of the day. Muqatil said: what is meant by it is the prayer of 'Asr, which is the Middle Prayer that Allah, glorified is He, commanded to be guarded. It was also said that it is an oath by the 'asr of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Zajjaj said: some of them said its meaning is "By the Lord of al-'Asr," but the first is more preferable.

﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss.﴾ This is the response to the oath.

Al-khusr and al-khusran are deficiency and the loss of capital. The meaning is that every human being, in trade, in endeavours, and in spending lifetimes on the affairs of this world, is in deficiency and in error away from the truth until he dies.

It was said that what is meant by al-insan is the disbeliever, and it was said that it refers to a group of the disbelievers: they are al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Asad. The first is more preferable, because of the generality contained in the word al-insan and because of the indication of the exception.

Al-Akhfash said: "in loss" means in ruin.

Al-Farra' said: punishment.

Ibn Zayd said: in evil.

The majority read "wal-'asr" with the sad sukun.

They also read "khusr" with a damma on the kha' and sukun on the sin.

Yahya ibn Salam read "wal-'asir" with a kasra on the sad.

Al-A'raj, Talhah, and 'Isa read "khusur" with a damma on the kha' and the sin, and this reading is narrated from 'Asim.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds.﴾ That is, they combined faith in Allah and righteous action, so they are in gain, not in loss, because they worked for the Hereafter and the affairs of this world did not preoccupy them from it. The exception is contiguous (muttasil). As for the one who said that what is meant by al-insan is only the disbeliever, then the exception is disconnected (munqati'), and every believing man and woman falls under this exception. There is no basis for what was said, that what is meant is the Companions or some of them, for the wording is general, and no one who is characterized by faith and righteous action is excluded from it. ﴿And they enjoined one another to the truth.﴾ That is, some of them advised others to the truth that is binding to uphold, which is faith in Allah and monotheism, upholding what Allah has legislated, and avoiding what He has forbidden.

Qatadah said: "the truth" means the Qur'an. It was also said it means monotheism, and taking it in its general sense is more preferable. ﴿And they enjoined one another to patience.﴾ That is, to patience in refraining from the disobedience of Allah, glorified is He, and patience in performing His obligations.

The placing of mutual enjoining to patience alongside mutual enjoining to the truth is evidence of its great worth, its lofty nobility, and the abundant reward of the patient in what patience is due for, ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153]. Also, enjoining one another to patience is among what falls under enjoining one another to the truth, so singling it out for mention and specifying it by explicit text is among the greatest proofs indicating its superiority over the qualities of truth, its added nobility over them, and the elevation of its rank above them.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿wal-'asr﴾, that he said: "It is al-dahr."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: "It is an hour of the hours of the day."

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him that he said: "It is the time before the setting of the sun, of the evening."

Al-Firyabi and Abu 'Ubayd in his Fada'il, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he used to recite: "Wal-'asr, wa nawa'ib al-dahr, inna al-insana lafi khusr, wa innahu fihi ila akhir al-dahr."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to recite: "Wal-'asr," "Inna al-insana lafi khusr," and "wa innahu lafihi ila akhir al-dahr." Ended.
